summary: Defines how to represent the X.400 O/R Address hierarchy in the X.500 Directory Information Tree. It is experimental and was replaced by RFC 2294.

plainLanguage.summary: A way to file email addresses in the big directory as folders within folders.

subtitle: Map X.400 email addresses to the X.500 directory tree structure.

tldr.problem: X.400 message systems use O/R (Originator/Recipient) addresses with a hierarchical structure, but X.500 is a separate directory system. To route and map addresses between X.400 and X.500, there must be a way to represent O/R Address hierarchies in the X.500 Directory Information Tree.
tldr.mechanism: Define X.500 object classes and attributes that correspond to each level of the O/R Address hierarchy (country, ADMD, PRMD, organization, organizational units, person, etc.), allowing mechanical transformation in both directions.
tldr.outcome: Systems can now store X.400 addresses in X.500 directories and look them up or map between the two systems. This RFC is experimental and was replaced by RFC 2294.

facts.label: Object classes defined
facts.value: 11 (country, ADMD, PRMD, organization, unit, person, named object, terminal, and others)

today: RFC 1836 is an Experimental protocol, superseded by RFC 2294. The representation of X.400 addresses in X.500 directories continues to be standardized, building on the foundation defined here.

sections.title: The O/R Address Hierarchy
sections.content:
X.400 message systems use O/R addresses (Originator/Recipient addresses) to identify senders and recipients. An O/R Address is composed of components arranged in a strict hierarchy: Country (C), ADMD (Administration Management Domain, typically a national post office), PRMD (Private Management Domain, a private network), Organization (O), Organizational Units (OU), Person (a personal name), and optional attributes like X.121 terminal identifiers.

X.500 is a global directory service that organizes entries in a Directory Information Tree (DIT) using a hierarchical structure. The problem is bridging these two systems: how to represent the X.400 O/R Address structure within an X.500 directory, enabling X.500 directory services to support MHS (Message Handling System) routing and X.400/RFC 822 address mappings.

The RFC defines a set of X.500 object classes and attributes that map to each O/R Address component. By arranging these object classes in the X.500 tree in the same order as the O/R Address components, a mechanical transformation becomes possible: any X.400 O/R Address can be converted to an X.500 distinguished name and back.
sections.plainLanguage: X.400 addresses are like a postal address: country, post office, company, department, person. X.500 is a directory organized the same way. This RFC defines which X.500 folders store which address parts, so you can look up an X.400 address in X.500.

sections.title: Object Classes and the Address Hierarchy
sections.content:
The RFC defines eleven X.500 object classes corresponding to the levels of an O/R Address. From top to bottom: mHSCountry (for country level, based on the standard country object class), aDMD (Administration Management Domain), pRMD (Private Management Domain), mHSOrganization, mHSOrganizationalUnit, mHSPerson, mHSNamedObject, mHSTerminalID, mHSX121 (X.121 terminal addresses), and mHSDomainDefinedAttribute.

Each object class has required attributes that provide the naming component. For example, mHSCountry requires countryName or mHSNumericCountryName, and mHSOrganization requires mHSOrganizationName. A given object class will always be higher in the DIT than object classes defined lower in the hierarchy. This strict ordering ensures that the tree structure mirrors the O/R Address hierarchy, making the transformation mechanical and reversible.

The RFC includes specific rules: Domain Defined Attributes (DDAs) are represented as multi-valued RDNs (Relative Distinguished Names) with type and value components. Personal names are also multi-valued RDNs with surname, given name, initials, and generation qualifier. When both Printable String and T.61 (Teletex) encodings exist in an O/R Address, both must be present in the X.500 tree, with one as an alias for the other.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC creates X.500 folders for each part of an address: folders for country, post office, company, department, person. Each folder type can only go inside certain other folders, just like in X.400. So any X.400 address fits naturally into X.500.

sections.title: Mapping Between O/R Address and Distinguished Name
sections.content:
The transformation from X.400 O/R Address to X.500 Distinguished Name (DN) is mechanical. The O/R Address is treated as an ordered list according to Table 1 of the RFC (Country, ADMD, PRMD, Organization, Organizational Units, Person, Named Object, Terminal ID, X.121, Domain Defined Attributes). For each component, the equivalent X.500 naming attribute is generated. For most components, the mapping is straightforward: O=Company becomes mHSOrganizationName; OU=Department becomes mHSOrganizationalUnitName.

The reverse mapping from X.500 DN to O/R Address is also mechanically reversible because all naming attributes are unique. If an O/R Address contains only higher-level components (for example, just country, ADMD, and organization), the X.500 directory returns the longest possible match. Personal names and Domain Defined Attributes, which have multiple components, are represented as multi-valued RDNs; the RFC specifies how to map these.

The RFC notes that only certain forms of O/R Address are mapped this way: mnemonic form (using text names), numeric form (using country codes and digits), and terminal forms using X.121 addressing for fax. Physical delivery addresses and other terminal or network address forms are handled by separate Access Unit mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: You can convert an X.400 address to X.500 by going through it left to right, converting each part to the matching X.500 folder name. You can also go backwards: from X.500 folders back to an X.400 address. If the address is incomplete, X.500 gives you the best match it can find.

sections.title: Notation and Examples
sections.content:
An X.400 O/R Address is written using X.400 notation. For example: I=S; S=Kille; OU1=CS; O=UCL, P=UK.AC; A=Gold 400; C=GB breaks down as Initial S, Surname Kille, Organization Unit CS, Organization UCL, PRMD UK.AC, ADMD Gold 400, Country GB.

This address is represented in X.500 with string representation of distinguished names using keywords defined by the RFC. The mHSInitials attribute uses the keyword MHS-I, the surname uses MHS-S, organizational unit uses MHS-OU, and so on. The example O/R Address above becomes: MHS-I=S + MHS-S=Kille, MHS-OU=CS, MHS-O=UCL, PRMD=UK.AC, ADMD=Gold 400, C=GB in X.500 notation.

The RFC includes tables mapping X.400 components (like C, A, P, O, OU, PN, CN) to their corresponding X.500 object classes and naming attributes, allowing for straightforward conversion between the two representations.
sections.plainLanguage: X.400 writes addresses in shorthand: I=S means initial S, S=Kille means surname Kille. X.500 writes them as folders: MHS-I=S, MHS-S=Kille inside an MHS-O folder inside an ADMD folder inside a C (country) folder. The mapping is one-to-one.
